text: A friend of mine in the East. <break time="0.8s" /> Once wrote to me. <break time="0.8s" /> And asked me to visit. <break time="0.8s" /> An old man named Simon Wheeler. <break time="0.8s" /> He wanted me to ask Wheeler. <break time="0.8s" /> About his childhood friend. <break time="0.8s" /> The Reverend Leonidas W, Smiley. <break time="0.8s" /> Later I began to suspect. <break time="0.8s" /> That there was no such person. <break time="0.8s" /> And that my friend had played a trick on me. <break time="0.8s" /> He probably guessed that if I asked about Leonidas. <break time="0.8s" /> Wheeler would remember a man named Jim Smiley. <break time="0.8s" /> And bore me nearly to death. <break time="0.8s" /> I found Simon Wheeler. <break time="0.8s" /> Dozing comfortably by the stove. <break time="0.8s" /> In an old tavern. <break time="0.8s" /> In the mining camp of Angels. <break time="0.8s" /> He was fat and bald. <break time="0.8s" /> And he had a gentle and simple look. <break time="0.8s" /> On his calm face. <break time="0.8s" /> When I told him the reason. <break time="0.8s" /> Why I had come. <break time="0.8s" /> He backed me into a corner. <break time="0.8s" /> And blocked me there with his chair. <break time="0.8s" /> Then he sat down. <break time="0.8s" /> And began a long story. <break time="0.8s" /> Which he told without smiling once. <break time="0.8s" /> Or changing his quiet, gentle voice. <break time="0.8s" /> He seemed to believe. <break time="0.8s" /> That the story was truly important. <break time="0.8s" /> And that its two heroes. <break time="0.8s" /> Were men of great genius. <break time="0.8s" /> To me. <break time="0.8s" /> The funniest thing was the way he told such a silly story so seriously. <break time="0.8s" /> So I let him go on without interrupting.
